name: Chasta Costa
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Sapir, Edward. 1914. Notes on Chasta Costa Phonology and Morphology. University of Pennsylvania, The University Museum, Anthropological Publications II(2): 271-340. (archive.org Cornell scan cu31924027107741)
catalog_locator: p. 276 (Phonology: vocalic quantity) with footnote 7; cf. p. 329 with footnote
catalog_quote: In general, however, stress accent cannot be said to be particularly well marked in Chasta Costa.⁷ Each syllable is a fairly well-defined phonetic unit tending to hold its own against others, so that an approximately level accentual flow with but few peaks results. Such writings as nā/dít/t!ō and tc!ā/θíl/se, with apparent accent preceded by long vowels, are doubtless but imperfect renderings of forms with level stress on first and second syllables (they might perhaps better be written nå/dìt/t!ō and tc!å/θìl/se with secondary accent on second syllable). [fn. 7] Weak stress accent seems characteristic of Athabascan generally. Father Morice goes so far as to say, "there is no accent in Déné" (op. cit., p. 173). [p. 329, on prefix-vowel quantity alternations:] It is very likely that we are dealing here primarily with considerations of syllabic and quantitative rhythm or balance. [fn.] Hardly stress accent as such. I cannot help feeling that such rhythmic phenomena will turn out to be of fundamental importance for Athabascan generally.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Sapir reports no well-marked word stress in Chasta Costa: syllables are roughly equally prominent ('level accentual flow with but few peaks'); the accents he transcribed on syllables following long-vowel prefixes he reinterprets as level stress over the first two syllables, and stem-vowel quantity alternations he attributes to syllabic/quantitative rhythm rather than stress (p. 329 fn.). No positional stress rule is given.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only the remark that forms like nā/dít/t!ō might better be written with 'secondary accent on second syllable', i.e. level stress across syllables 1-2; no systematic secondary-stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Same page: long prefix vowels may shorten when 'immediately followed or preceded by a syllable with relatively strong accent' (e.g. łá na/dit/t!ō, where na/dit/t!ō is 'phonetically enclitic to strongly accented łá'), so some syllables (particles, stems) do carry relatively strong accent; Sapir gives no rule for where.
new_statements.domain_note: Impressionistic description of isolated words and short verb forms from a single speaker recorded in 1906; word-level, citation forms. No tone is described for Chasta Costa.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is Sapir's description of Chasta Costa (Šista Qʼʷə́sta, Illinois River), recorded 1906 at Siletz from one speaker. Glottolog 5.1 gives Chasta Costa no separate code and files Sapir 1914 under tutu1242 (Tututni has no dialect children there); Golla 1976/2011 and Wikipedia treat Chasta Costa as a dialect of Tututni / Lower Rogue River. The statement is therefore a dialect-level description, not one of Tututni proper (Tututunne/Joshua/Mikwanutunne).

tone_statements.citation: Krauss, Michael E. 2005 [written 1979]. Athabaskan Tone. In Sharon Hargus & Keren Rice (eds.), Athabaskan Prosody (Current Issues in Linguistic Theory 269), 55-136. Amsterdam/Philadelphia: John Benjamins. [Read in the open typescript 'Athabaskan Tone', October 1979, 2003 retyping, 72 pp., Alaska Native Language Archive item CA961K1978.]
tone_statements.quote: Sapir’s first field encounter with Athabaskan was in 1906 with Chasta Costa, toneless like all PCA. [...] [sec. 7.2:] Of the rest of the Athabaskan languages, Babine-Hagwilgate in Canada (on evidence from James Kari) and in Alaska, Ahtna, Tanaina, Ingalik, Upper Kuskowin and the Central and Upper dialects Koyukon are definitely toneless, along with PCA, Kwalhioqua-Tlatskanai (and Eyak). Eyak, PCA, probably Kw-Tl, Ahtna, and Tanaina have kept much of the stem-final stop glottalization, and (except for Tanaina) glottal stop.

tone_statements.citation: Leer, Jeff. 1999. Tonogenesis in Athabaskan. In Shigeki Kaji (ed.), Proceedings of the Symposium Cross-Linguistic Studies of Tonal Phenomena: Tonogenesis, Typology, and Related Topics (Tokyo, December 10-12, 1998), 37-66. Tokyo: Institute for the Study of Languages and Cultures of Asia and Africa (ILCAA), Tokyo University of Foreign Studies.
tone_statements.quote: Among North American Indian languages, Athabaskan is the family best known for its tone languages. To be sure, not all Athabaskan languages are tone languages; about half of the Athabaskan languages of Alaska, a couple of the Athabaskan languages of British Columbia, and all of the Pacific Coast Athabaskan languages are known not to have tone systems at all, or to have only vestigial tone systems. Nevertheless, by far the majority of extant Athabaskan languages have fully functional tone systems, many with only two tones, but some with three or even four monomoraic tones.
tone_statements.n_tones: 0 (no tone system, or vestigial at most, for PCA as a group)

tone_statements.citation: Hoijer, Harry. 1960. Athapaskan languages of the Pacific Coast. In Stanley Diamond (ed.), Culture in History: Essays in Honor of Paul Radin, 960-976. New York: Columbia University Press.
tone_statements.quote: It might be noted, however, that none of the Pacific Coast languages so far studied possess tone phonemes. These have been found in all the Apachean languages and in Sarci, Chipewyan, Hare, and Kutchin of the north. Data on the remaining northern languages are uncertain on this point, but there is reason to believe that tone phonemes may be discovered in all of them. It follows, then, that this point has significance in setting the Pacific Coast languages apart from the rest. [...] (p. 969) For point (1) we may cite: (a) the absence of pitch accent in PCA (§ 2)
tone_statements.locator: pp. 963-964, end of section II; restated p. 969, Summary point (1)(a)
